science.text: Research indicates that nine large tsunamigenic landslides struck Sullorsuaq Strait in Greenland during prehistoric times in the Holocene. Seven came from the southern coast of the Nuussuaq Peninsula and two from the northern coast of Disko Island.

Around the end of the 8th millennium BC, the Holocene Climate Optimum began, a warm period lasting roughly 4,000 years until about 3000 BC. Summer sunlight in the northern hemisphere was unusually strong. This brought pronounced warming to high latitudes such as Greenland, and a reduction in Arctic sea ice.

Estimates vary for when the Arctic was last ice-free, from 65 million years ago, when fossils indicate plants existed there, to as recently as 5,500 years ago. Ice and ocean cores going back 8,000 years are cited for the last warm period.

Geologists call the first stage of the Holocene the Greenlandian, running from about 9700 BC to 6236 BC. It followed the Younger Dryas and featured a climate shift from near-glacial to interglacial conditions. Glaciers retreated and sea levels rose.
Seven of the prehistoric landslides in Sullorsuaq Strait apparently occurred between about 8020 BC and 6520 BC. Their tsunamigenic effects are unidentified.

The authors of the 2014 study suggested that the ancestors of the Saqqaq and Dorset entered North America from Siberia in a single distinct migration about 4000 BCE. After that they remained genetically largely isolated for thousands of years. The Thule people later completely replaced the Dorset around 1300 CE.
One of the two most recent prehistoric landslides generated a megatsunami that struck Alluttoq Island around 5650 BC. Its run-up height was 41 to 66 metres (135 to 217 ft).
Another megatsunami struck Alluttoq Island around 5350 BC, following the earlier one at about 5650 BC. Its run-up height was 45 to 70 metres (148 to 230 ft), slightly higher than the first.

culture.text: The Komsa culture was a Mesolithic culture of hunter-gatherers that existed from around 10,000 BC in Northern Norway. It is known for a type of stone-tool culture found north of the Arctic Circle.

The Komsa are thought to have followed the Norwegian coastline as receding glaciation at the end of the last ice age, between 11,000 and 8000 BC, opened up new areas for settlement. The earliest settlement of the North Norwegian coast is thought to trace back to the final Palaeolithic Ahrensburg culture of northwestern Europe.

Around 4000 BCE, the ancestors of the Paleo-Eskimos migrated from Siberia to North America in a distinct migration, after which they remained genetically largely isolated. The first known Paleo-Eskimo culture, the Early Paleo-Eskimo, had developed by 3900 to 3600 BCE.
Anthropologists believe the common ancestors of the Inuit and related peoples originated in eastern Siberia. They arrived in the Bering Sea area approximately 10,000 years ago.

The first Inuit group, known as the Paleo-Eskimos, crossed the Bering Strait in 3000 BCE, presumably on winter ice. This came long after earlier migrations by the ancestors of the North American Indians.

The Komsa culture is named after Mount Komsa in Alta Municipality, Finnmark, where its remains were first found. Archaeologist Anders Nummedal first used the term after his discoveries there in 1925. A supposed split between a northern Komsa type and a Fosna type from Trøndelag to Oslofjord was rendered obsolete in the 1970s.

Finds from Finnish Lapland were once thought to be an inland part of the Komsa culture. They are now linked to the Post-Swiderian culture of North Central Russia and the eastern Baltic, and so represent a separate early incursion into northernmost Scandinavia. Some Varangerfjord sites once attributed to Komsa are also thought to reflect this influx.
